awd_titl_txt: Collaborative Research: RUI: IRES Track 1: Empowering students to bridge the gap between hydrologic science and community resilience: A case study in post-glacial Perú
awd_abstract_narration:
Solutions to water resources management and water security require not only fundamentally sound science, but also a diverse coalition of trained scientists that recognizes and is aware of the needs and knowledge of local communities. Through our IRES award, we will train three cohorts of ten U.S. students from the Hispanic Serving Institutions of Humboldt State University (HSU) and Rutgers University, Newark (RUN) in applied, interdisciplinary and community-based water development. Each cohort will participate in a yearlong program consisting of three components: (1) a spring preparatory course which will link students from HSU and RUN via videoconferencing to their Peruvian peers; (2) a five-week hydrogeophysical field campaign centered in two communities in the Cusco region of Perú and led by an interdisciplinary team of U.S. and Peruvian scholars; and (3) a fall semester of independent research. The experience will empower a diverse cohort of students to be interdisciplinary and community-minded scientists as well as train members of the local communities to collect hydrologic data in order to guide best practices in water management and increase local water security and resiliency. 

The puna biome, a seasonally dry grass and shrub ecosystem at the altitudinal limits of plant growth in the central Andes, provides the primary source of water to many small agrarian communities and large cities, such as Cusco. Despite its importance for water resources, however, the hydrology of the puna is poorly understood, especially with regard to storage capacity and seasonal runoff dynamics. Communities relying on puna derived water sources are thus potentially vulnerable to changes in water supply and uninformed water management decisions. We will guide students in a hydrologic, geologic and geophysical investigation to quantify water resources and flow pathways in two small (~ 2.2 km2) ‘end-member’ puna catchments. In one catchment, slow drainage from peat forming wetlands, known locally as bofedales, sustains perennial streamflow which supports community agriculture. In the other catchment, devoid of bofedales, stream flow is ephemeral, however the community harvests fracture flow for agricultural and municipal water use via a 140 m long tunnel. Our results will quantify water resources in puna landscapes with and without the influence of bofedales, inform model predictions of future changes in water resources, and guide community-based best practices in land and water management.

This award reflects NSF's statutory mission and has been deemed worthy of support through evaluation using the Foundation's intellectual merit and broader impacts review criteria.

por.por_cntn:
Water security is one of the most pressing environmental problems across both the developing and developed world. In Perú, the Andes mountains catch passing moisture which is stored and released to millions of people from the moist Amazon basin to the arid coast. Although the Andes are home to the highest concentration of the world’s tropical glaciers, these glaciers occupy a relatively small and shrinking portion of the mountain range. Recent research highlights the importance of the humid puna, a seasonally dry grass and shrub-land, in regulating water yield to sustain perennial streams through the annual 5-month dry season. Although the humid puna is the primary water source for Cusco (pop. 428,000), the largest city in the Perúvian Andes, scarce hydrologic data to constrain hydrologic models limits the ability of decision makers to achieve water security. By introducing students to and exploring scientific questions around understanding and quantifying water storage and availability in the humid puna biome, our project aimed to bridge gaps between science and society with the following goals: 1) quantify water resources in the Cusco region and explore the hydrologic regulation capacity of bofedales, or peat-forming wetlands, 2) collaborate with local communities to develop approaches to water resources management spanning the vertical kilometer between upstream water sources and their downstream water needs, and 3) recruit a multicultural cohort of hydrogeologists, engineers, and social scientists and train these students to be the interdisciplinary and community focused scientists of tomorrow.

 

Scientific Merit

Our research focused primarily on quantifying water resources in the Upper Ramuschaka Watershed (URW) (2.12 km2) which provides water for the agrarian village of Zurite in the Department of Cusco. The URW is a typical ‘post-glacial’ watershed with steep amphitheater shaped uplands covered primarily in native bunchgrasses and low-gradient interior basins covered in seasonally saturated bofedales. Bofedales cover 12 % of the URW. We installed long-term hydrologic monitoring equipment to measure dynamics in precipitation, subsurface moisture, evapotranspiration, groundwater, and streamflow. Extensive geophysical datasets – including electrical resistivity, time domain induced polarization, and ground penetrating radar –  were collected over five bofedales to explore subsurface structure, quantify dynamic moisture storage, and define hydrologic pathways from hillslopes through bofedales to streams. Thus far, we have quantified the important role bofedales play in sustaining dry season streamflow, detailed our approach to knowledge co-production involving students faculty and the community of Zurite. Ongoing projects are focused on revealing the subsurface structure and properties of hillslopes connecting hillslopes to bofedales, quantifying bofedal recharge via springs, and a comparison of aquifer recharge below native grasslands and native forest. Collectively, these datasets have contributed to our understanding of bofedal formation and function, as well as our hydrologic understanding of the societally important humid puna.  

Broader Impacts

Across the 3 years of this project, we have trained over 30 students primarily from Rutgers University, Newark and Cal Poly Humboldt. In each year of the project students participated in a semester-long seminar building scientific skills in hydrology, geophysics, and water resource engineering, studying the societal and scientific context for water resources in the Perúvian Andes, and developing cultural awareness and competency. Throughout this first semester, students develop a research project and a data collection plan for field work in Perú. We guided field investigations and cultural learning over a four- to five-week long immersive research experience in the Cusco region where students lived in local villages, collaborated with students from universities across Perú and implemented their proposed research. Following the research experience, we guided student research and collaborative knowledge production through a semester-long seminar. Students analyzed data, made interpretations, developed writing and speaking skills, and presented their work within socio-hydrological context of water resources challenges in Andean Perú. Students presented their work in oral and written modes to the class and many presented their work at intramural conferences or international conferences such as the American Geophysical Union Fall Conference. Through this multi-semester approach, students were supported to build skills positioning them to become leaders in international water resources research. Survey results show the impact of our program in reinforcing student interest in water resources, validating students as scientists, and boosting confidence in pursuing careers in research.
